meaning: male fertility deity in Hawaiian mythology

phonemes.desc: Voiceless velar plosive [k] plus pure [a] — Hawaiian k is crisp and unaspirated.
Bilabial nasal [m] plus [a] — the syllable of kama, 'child.'
Bilabial [p] plus the vowels pu-a-a: pua'a is the pig — the name's whole second half, and its meaning.

pronunciation.approximation: 'kah-mah-POO-ah-ah' — five light syllables; stress on the pu, and let the final a-a sound as two separate vowels.

kin.label: Name
kin.form: Hawaiian kama 'child' + pua'a 'pig' — 'pig-child,' the name as a program

kin.label: Mother
kin.form: Hina — his mother in the O'ahu cycle, one of the great Hinas of Polynesian myth (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology)

kin.label: Rival-wife
kin.form: Pele — the volcano goddess he courted, flooded, and married in the great island cycle

pronunciation.note: Kamapua'a is the Hawaiian pig-god of O'ahu; the lexicon keeps the older missionary-era spelling, in which the ʻokina is unwritten. No vowel length marks the name: Tier 2, a display fact only. His name is his biography — kama 'child,' pua'a 'pig' — and his myth makes both halves true.

domains.title: Kamapuaa
domains.subtitle: Pig God
domains.lead: Kamapua'a is the pig-god of O'ahu — shape-shifter, ravager of plantations, master of rain and flood, and the only suitor who ever beat Pele at her own element. He is agriculture's wild side: the animal that roots up the garden, and the storm that waters it.

cards.name: The Shape-Shifter
cards.desc: Man and hog and fog: he changed form at will, and his tusk-furrows became the valleys of O'ahu's Ko'olau range.

cards.name: The Hog of Kaliuwa'a
cards.desc: Born in the sheer valley of Kaliuwa'a — Sacred Falls — to the goddess Hina; the cliffs are still his birthplace.

cards.name: Lord of Cultivars
cards.desc: He stole and spread the garden's wealth — taro, yam, gourd — and finally bargained Pele's lava away from the farms.

cards.name: The Flood That Courted Fire
cards.desc: He wooed Pele with rain until her fires hissed; their marriage joined storm and volcano in treaty.

symbols.name: The boar's tusk
symbols.meaning: His tusks furrowed the valleys; pig-tooth ornaments (niho pua'a) worn by chiefs carried his mana.

symbols.name: Kaliuwa'a — Sacred Falls
symbols.meaning: The sheer-walled valley of his birth, closed to entry under old custom — a sanctuary the myth still owns.

symbols.name: The rain
symbols.meaning: His element of courtship and war: he came to Pele as fog, rain, and thunderstorm, and water is how he wins.

symbols.name: The spring
symbols.meaning: Where his tusks struck the rock, fresh water broke forth — the wild hog as water-bringer.

symbols.name: The cultivated field
symbols.meaning: The garden he ravaged and then defended: his cycle ends as god of agriculture, not only of its destruction.

mythology.lead: Kamapua'a's cycle, best preserved in the O'ahu traditions Beckwith summarized and Westervelt printed, is a trickster epic with a strange ending: the ravager marries the destroyer, and the islands get a farm treaty.

myths.title: The Child of the Cliffs
myths.text: Kamapua'a was born in Kaliuwa'a, the sheer valley of the Ko'olau range on O'ahu — the valley the Hawaiians call Sacred Falls — to the goddess Hina. From the first he was double: a child who was also a hog, fair-faced as a young chief, yet able to swell into an enormous boar whose bristles swept the ferns. He grew among the cliff country of the windward coast, and the cycle follows him as he raids the coastal plantations — pulling up taro and yam, devouring or carrying off the stored wealth of the district — while the farmers' traps and the chiefs' hunters fail against an animal that is also a man. (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Gods and Ghosts.) The myth's heart is in the name itself: kama, child; pua'a, pig — the beloved and the pest as one being, as any farmer who has watched a feral boar in the taro already knows.

myths.title: The Chiefs Who Could Not Catch a God
myths.text: The raids brought the hunt. The chiefs of the coast — in the longer versions led by 'Olopana, lord of the district — pursued the sacred hog into the mountains with spears, ropes, and traps, and Kamapua'a made fools of every formation: he vanished into fog, doubled back as a handsome stranger who ate at the pursuers' own fires by night, and was the boar again bursting their cordons by day. The versions collected in the nineteenth century delight in these escapes — the hog bleeding one moment into mist, the next a man laughing on the cliff — and they end the same way: the hunters quit, and the hog keeps the mountain. (Fornander, An Account of the Polynesian Race; Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology.) What reads as a folk tale of an uncatchable pig is a charter: the uplands belong to the wild thing, and human order stops at the tree-line.

myths.title: Rain on the Volcano
myths.text: Then Kamapua'a came down the island chain to Pele. She mocked him as a hog, and he answered with his other nature: he wrapped Kīlauea in fog, drowned its fires in rain, and thundered at the crater until the volcano hissed and steamed in its own pit — the first power in the islands to beat Pele at her own game. At the height of the storm the cycle turns: Pele, outmatched, yields, and the hog and the volcano marry — fire taking water for its mate. (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Westervelt, Hawaiian Legends of Volcanoes.) The courtship is the cycle's masterpiece of imagery: the flood that courts the volcano — water proposing to fire, and fire, astonishingly, accepting.

myths.title: What the Marriage Settled
myths.text: The marriage was a constitution. By its terms, the cycle says, Pele's lava would keep to the forests and the uplands and leave the cultivated lowlands to live; and Kamapua'a's rains would water the farms and fatten the gardens he had once ravaged. The boar who destroyed plantations became the god who protects them — agriculture's own dangerous patron, the wild force inside cultivation that must be married, not killed. In the closing chapters he returns to O'ahu and to his mother Hina, honored as a god of plenty, his feral children the pigs of the mountain and his gentler children the crops of the field. (Beckwith, Hawaiian Mythology; Kamakau, Ka Moolelo Hawaii.) The myth understands something modern conservation is relearning: the destructive force is not the enemy of the garden but its spouse — and the only bad outcome is war without a treaty.

lore.syncretism: Kamapua'a is Hawaiian to the bone — the pig has no pan-Polynesian divine twin of quite his kind, though the boar figures everywhere in island myth and tabu — and his nearest relations are local: his mother Hina, the great Polynesian goddess the Hawaiians multiplied into a dozen local Hinas, and his wife-rival Pele, whose cycle absorbs his. The nineteenth century treated him as a curiosity, and the early tale-collectors printed him as a marvel-story; Beckwith restored him to seriousness as the agricultural meaning of the pig. In the modern renaissance he is claimed as the god of the Hawaiian rainforest and of the feral pig problem alike — the axis between conservation and subsistence hunting — and his name rides canoes, taro brands, and hālau. If Pele is the volcano that owns the land, Kamapua'a is the garden that owns its pest.
lore.culturalLegacy: Kamapua'a's legacy runs from the museum case to the dinner table. Pig remains dominate Hawaiian faunal assemblages from the earliest settlement layers — the pig was the islanders' principal meat and most prestigious offering, which is why a pig-god could carry chiefly mana. Pig-tusk ornaments, documented by Kamakau and preserved in the earliest contact-period collections in London and Honolulu, attest his prestige in chiefly dress. Sacred Falls — Kaliuwa'a — was closed to visitors after fatalities in the 1990s and remains kapu, a closure many Hawaiians frame as the valley reasserting his tapu. Taro farmers invoke him wryly: taro is his stolen treasure that became the staff of life. And the courtship cycle is performed still — the flood wooing the fire is one of the great set-pieces of Hawaiian storytelling, a comic epic that ends, unusually for a trickster, in a working marriage.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Every agricultural people knows the animal in Kamapua'a: the creature that is wealth and destruction in one body — the pig that manures the field and roots it up, the rain that drowns the seedlings and fills the pond. What Hawaiian myth did with that knowledge is marry it. The boar does not get exterminated in this cycle; he gets married to the volcano and bound by treaty. It is among the most sophisticated land-use stories in this catalog: destruction domesticated not by force but by alliance, the pest made a spouse with terms.

There is a gentler reading too. Kamapua'a is the child no one wanted — half pig, born in the least approachable valley on the island — who grows up to be the one being Pele cannot defeat. The despised form conceals the effective nature. His cycle tells every misfit with a stubborn streak what the tradition believes: you are not the problem; you are the untried element, and the day will come when even the volcano needs rain.

lore.archaeology: Kamapua'a's material traces are modest but real. Pig bones dominate Hawaiian faunal assemblages from the earliest settlement layers — the pig was the islanders' principal meat and most prestigious sacrifice, which is why a pig-god could carry chiefly mana. Pig-tusk ornaments (niho pua'a), worn as anklets and necklaces by the ali'i, are well represented in contact-period museum collections. Kaliuwa'a, the sheer valley of his birth, shows no monumental works — Hawaiian gods kept open-air shrines — but its waterfalls, pools, and cliff walls were the sanctuary itself, and its modern closure to the public has made it again what the myth says it always was: his valley, closed.
